McBehrer:

If you want to play a superhero-based deckbuilder, play Legendary. It's MUCH MUCH better. DC isn't really that great of a game. Plus Legendary has expansions, and actually represents the theme well.

I agree that Legendary is a vastly better game than DCH, but it is not better for the purpose of providing light entertainment to non-gamers.  The setup time alone would make people wander away in boredom, and the technicalities of the game, the effort of playing a new villain card every turn, the need for heroes to work together to avoid an Evil Wins event but also competing amongst each other for the individual victory…it'd definitely have a lot of potential to turn a newbie off.  Like I said before, DCH is a gateway game; it's not great in the long term, but it can give people a good starting point.

Gislef:

They also have an attack mechanism that "fights back," which except for… four? villains, all other cards lack.

Yes, that mechanic comes into effect after you buy the card.  So, when Scarecrow is running around in the world, he's completely harmless; only after Superman "buys" him does he start frightening all the other superheroes.  It's not great flavor for a superhero game.

Villain card order can be chosen if random selection is considered inadequate.

Nothing in the rules suggests this.  Certainly it's something a playgroup could decide to do, but the game itself isn't printed in a way that facilitates this, as the LOTR DBGs are.

In the comics, Green Lantern uses his power ring

Yeah I know, I'm not saying it isn't fitting.  I'm just saying that, mechanically, Green Lantern doesn't tell you what cards to buy (other than non-duplicates) the way all of the other heroes (even the promo Martian Manhunter) do.  This is what I call "linearity", meaning that the game itself tells you what to do in order to succeed in it; it's a very valuable trait in games aimed at a casual audience, while being largely counterproductive to hardcore gamers.  The counterpart trait that they look for is "modularity", and DCH is fairly horrible about that, which is why I think most players will outgrow it.

Aquaman, Wonder Woman

Yeah, I never mentioned them.  They have linearity, and even Flash does a little

danmarshall14:

King of Tokyo is always a good pick for newcomers. Just make sure you’re playing with other people who make it fun. Last time I tried to get a non-gamer into games via King of Tokyo, she thought it was incredibly boring because the other players were incredibly serious about it and took like 30 seconds in between each roll to figure out their most optimum strategy. It’s like “Dude…just roll the damn dice. It’s supposed to be a light, fast paced game.” There’s a time for being competitive; playing King of Tokyo with a few first-timers who are trying to get into tabletop gaming is not one of those times.Dominion is very good for introducing card playing mechanics to newcomers. The theme and elements are light enough for anyone to get into and it also features phases so they can get familiar with the concept of order of play. Just be careful: they might get so addicted to Dominion that they’ll never want to move on to Sentinels Red Dragon Inn, as you mentioned, is also a great beginner game. And like King of Tokyo, it really shines when people aren’t taking it too seriously and can just have fun. Most newcomers to board games don’t want to be competitive; that’s one of the biggest barriers to getting into tabletop.Smash Up! is also quite perfect. It’s incredibly light on mechanics (play a minion, play an action, draw 2), but has a lot of room for the play to begin to see “connections” and “combos” on their own without anyone holding their hand. After only playing a few rounds, they’ll begin to see moves they can make happen. “Oh, I see, I can play this zombie from my trash at the beginning of my turn for free, then use this minion who let’s me play an extra action, then use these two actions to…” That really creates a sense of having fun; being able to figure out how to play optimally on your own, and Smash Up! let’s players do that with ease. Plus who can argue to playing a game where Dinosaur Wizards fight Ninja Zombies? No one, that’s who.Now I’m going to throw out two games that a lot of hardcore tabletop gamers tend to absolute hate with a fiery passion. But hear me out. Those games are Munchkin and Fluxx (or Star Fluxx/other Fluxx theme). Now, I understand why gamers loathe these games, but putting that pure hatred aside, I think they can serve as great introductory games for the card-playing genre. It’s, again, the simple “Play a card, do what it says” element that these games do well (or in the case of Fluxx, completely uses it as a crutch to do whatever it wants). Plus, they are light and silly and can definitely serve as party games. I don’t think they should always hit the table; by all means Smash Up! does most of what these two do mechanically and is a much better game. But, if you’re playing with a player who really doesn’t take kindly to “rules” and the whole card-playing thing, these might be the good, fast paced drinking games that can serve as the gateway they need.

But that wouldn't be Carcassonne. Stealing is half of the point of the game - if you're not doing that you might as well play solo.

The point of Carcassone is that you're trying to find the best placement for each tile that you draw; it's an exercise in forging order out of chaos.  If people can steal your scoring areas, there's no point in bothering to build them up.  I would indeed rather play solo.

A good player will recognise when that might happen and change his play accordingly

This punishes a player for being unable to see such sneaky moves coming.  Hence my top-blowing.

or fight back by adding more of his own meeples

You have nowhere near enough meeples for this to be possible.  Particularly in H&G, you have only five meeples and the ones you place on Meadows are there until the end of the game.  You can't afford to waste two of them on securing a single Meadow, so if your opponent is able to patch into what you've built, both meeples are essentially negated, leaving fewer scoring opportunities and thus making the game even more luck-determined.
